notes: The classic, widely cited failsafe biasing derivation, originally National Semiconductor Application Note 847 and now archived under TI's literature number. Explains exactly why an idle or open RS-485 bus needs external pull up and pull down resistors and how to size them so the differential input threshold is never left in the indeterminate zone, a topic the Modbus spec mentions only in passing.

title: AN-1057 Ten Ways to Bulletproof RS-485 Interfaces
notes: A ten point field checklist covering termination, failsafe biasing, ground loops, common mode range, and ESD and surge protection in one short document. This is the one to hand a technician troubleshooting an intermittent RS-485 fault in the field, since it reads as a punch list rather than a derivation.

title: How to Isolate Signal and Power for an RS-485 System
notes: Short article on why and how to galvanically isolate an RS-485 node, covering both signal isolation and isolated power delivery, and the distinction between basic, reinforced, and functional isolation. Answers the ground loop and high voltage separation question that neither the Modbus spec nor the plain design guides above cover.

title: RS-485 Advanced Fail-Safe Feature Application Note
notes: Silicon vendor explanation of true failsafe receivers, the modern alternative to external bias resistors, including a device selection table and the internal circuit that pulls the receiver output high with no external biasing network. Useful for deciding whether a new transceiver design even needs the resistor math in the older TI and National Semiconductor notes.

title: RS-485 Transceivers in Fieldbus Networks Application Note
notes: Recent (2024) transceiver selection guide aimed specifically at fieldbus deployments, covering data rate versus cable length trade offs and multidrop network sizing from the silicon vendor's perspective rather than the standard's. Complements the older TI overview with a current parts landscape.

title: Enhanced Receiver Failsafe Implementation In Dual Protocol SP339 and XR34350 Serial Transceivers
notes: Narrow but concrete example of failsafe biasing for a dual protocol RS-232/RS-485/RS-422 transceiver, explaining why the external pull up and pull down jumpers used in RS-485 mode must be removed in RS-232 mode. Good for anyone dealing with a converter chip that switches between standards rather than a dedicated RS-485 line driver.

title: External Fail-Safe Biasing of RS-485 Networks
notes: Renesas's own worked derivation of the external bias resistor values needed on a noisy RS-485 network even when the transceiver already has integrated failsafe, explicitly framed as answering the single most common customer question the vendor receives. A third independent silicon vendor's math to cross check against TI and MaxLinear.

title: RS-422 & RS-485 Applications eBook: A Practical Guide To Using RS-422 and RS-485 Serial Interfaces
notes: A 100 page practical guide from a serial converter manufacturer (formerly B&B Electronics) that a Modbus or generic industrial spec never provides: two wire versus four wire wiring diagrams, ground loop avoidance, shield grounding at one point only, and converter specific troubleshooting. Written for installers, not chip designers, so it reads very differently from the transceiver vendor app notes above.

title: RS-485 Design and install best practices: Guidelines for successful communication
notes: A drive manufacturer's field install guide rather than a chip vendor's design guide, aimed at the embedded fieldbus ports on Variable Frequency Drives. Useful for the install context that most RS-485 physical layer documents skip: what actually goes wrong when a VFD's serial port is wired into a plant network, grounding practices around VFD chassis, and cable routing near motor drive noise sources.

title: Specification for SEMI Equipment Communications Standard 1 Message Transfer (SECS-I)
notes: The serial layer under SECS: point to point RS-232 between one host and one tool. This is the half that HSMS (E37) replaces, so read the two as a pair or neither makes sense. Sold as a single PDF download, 193 USD non member, 148 USD member. Current revision September 2023. The page publishes a free scope paragraph and nothing else of the text; the store's own title tag is truncated mid word, so the title here is transcribed from og:title, which is complete. GATED, UNREAD is the ceiling for this row: the document is paid and nobody here has opened it.

title: Specification for SEMI Equipment Communications Standard 2 Message Content (SECS-II)
notes: The message content: streams, functions, and the data item types. E5 is the part that SURVIVES a move from SECS-I to HSMS unchanged, which is exactly why the migration looks deceptively small before you start. Sold as a single PDF download, 380 USD non member; a Current plus Redline bundle is listed at 466 USD. Member price NOT recorded here: two independent reads of the page returned a member price higher than the non member price, which contradicts every other standard on this store and is almost certainly a parsing artifact rather than a fact. Current revision July 2025.

title: Specification for the Generic Model for Communications and Control of Manufacturing Equipment (GEM)
notes: The behaviour model on top of E5: state machines, collection events, alarms, remote commands. GEM is what a host actually integrates against, and it is the layer where two tools that both claim GEM still refuse to cooperate. Sold as a single PDF download, 380 USD non member, 286 USD member. Current revision May 2026, which is NEWER than any Wayback snapshot of this page: see the archive_url note in BACKLOG.md before trusting the snapshot to corroborate this revision.

title: Specification for High-Speed SECS Message Services (HSMS) Generic Services
notes: HSMS: SECS messages over TCP/IP, the replacement for SECS-I serial. The store's own free scope paragraph states it plainly, that HSMS is intended as an alternative to SEMI E4 (SECS-I) where higher speed communication is needed. Sold as a single PDF download, 380 USD non member. Current revision February 2022, and the page lists ten superseded revisions back to SEMI E37-95. This is the document at the centre of notes/secs-i-to-hsms (unwritten): the spec describes a correct migration and says nothing about how real ones fail, which is the entire reason that note has to exist and cannot be assembled out of documents.
